claims.claim: Literary analysis is a deep examination of a literary text that moves beyond retelling: it examines what is written (content) and how it is said (form and language) to develop an interpretation.

An interpretive thesis is a specific, debatable claim about what a text means or how it works; a sentence that only restates what happens is basically summary and is not debatable enough to drive an analysis.

Analytical interpretations are built around evidence from the text itself; a writer supports claims with textual evidence (paraphrase, summary, and direct quotation) and explains how that evidence supports the claim, because personal reaction alone cannot carry an argument.

A literary analysis essay has a recognizable structure: an introduction that gives context and presents the thesis, body paragraphs whose topic sentences and claims are supported by evidence, and a conclusion that restates the thesis in new words and extends to the work's significance or quality.

Simply paraphrasing the plot or content instead of analyzing it is a common weakness in student literary analyses; authors typically show a theme through story, character, and craft rather than stating it as a moral.

Textual analysis is about the meaning of the text and how the author created it, not about whether the reader likes the text; the analyst argues for one meaning rather than another possible meaning, using reasoning and textual evidence.

Close reading is the evidence-gathering practice that supplies the observations; literary analysis is the finished, thesis-driven argument that organizes those observations into claims about how the text creates meaning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Guides use 'literary analysis,' 'textual analysis,' and 'close reading' with overlapping meanings: one OER treats literary analysis and close reading as near-synonyms, while others treat close reading as one practice within the larger work of analysis.
positions: UNM Core Writing: 'Literary Analysis and Close Reading are two words with, for all intents and purposes, the same meaning,' with literary analysis specific to literature.
OpenStax Writing Guide: textual analysis is the broader work of developing and defending a thesis about a text's meaning, in which close attention to details supports the argument.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents close reading as the evidence-gathering practice and literary analysis as the completed interpretive argument, while noting that some materials use the terms interchangeably; the relationship is stated as complementary rather than identical.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Guidance on the conclusion differs: one source recommends restating the thesis and adding a broader statement, another recommends evaluating the work's quality and relevance.
positions: OpenStax: conclude by restating the thesis in different words and adding a general statement about the work and its significance.
UNM Core Writing: the conclusion presents an opinion on the quality of the work and comments on its current relevance.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says the conclusion returns to the thesis but does more than repeat it: it draws out what the analysis has shown, whether that is significance, quality, or consequences.

sourceRecords.title: Writing About Literature: What Makes a Good Literature Paper?
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports the argument-nature of literature papers, the requirement of a specific debatable thesis statement, and the contrast between a summary-level thesis ('a play about a young man who seeks revenge') and an interpretive one. Page carries an all-rights-reserved notice; facts were synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: 16.1 An Author's Choices: What Text Says and How It Says It
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly via curl. Supports textual analysis as the study of a text's meaning and how the author created it (not whether the reader likes it), and the instruction to develop a thesis and defend it with sound reasoning and convincing textual evidence. Page states it may not be used to train or ingest into generative AI; facts were synthesized without adapting source prose.

sourceRecords.title: 16.5 Writing Process: Thinking Critically About Text
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly via curl. Supports the components of a convincing textual analysis essay (overview, very brief summary, form and structure, point of view, context, and an assertion or thesis about what the text means as the analyst's main task), body paragraphs that refer to the thesis through topic sentences, a conclusion that restates the thesis and adds a statement about the work's significance, and the principle that analytical interpretations are built around evidence from the text itself. Page restricts LLM ingestion; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Literary Analysis — Write What Matters: CLC Edition
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports writing about literature as an exercise in critical thinking and communication, the need to examine a text both subjectively and objectively with facts from the text to support an argument (personal reaction alone is not enough), and theme as the heart of literature. No source wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Literary Analysis
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports literary analysis as deep examination of a work (content and form), the warning that paraphrasing the plot or content instead of analyzing it is a common weakness, theme as insight shown rather than told ('the moral of my story is' contrast), and essay structure: introduction with author/title/genre and a one-to-two-sentence statement of theme, body paragraphs that analyze how elements develop the theme, and a conclusion that evaluates quality and relevance. No source wording adapted.
